title: Remote Access Tools: Remote Access Hardware
shortTitle: Remote Access Tools: Remote Access Hardware
summary: Remote access hardware covers small physical devices that sit between a computer's keyboard, video and mouse connections and provide a network-accessible session, with IP-based keyboard, video and mouse appliances such as TinyPilot and PiKVM as the typical examples. Unlike the other remote access branches, nothing needs to run on the target operating system. The appliance presents itself to the host as ordinary input and display hardware, captures the video signal, and forwards input events, so it can reach a machine that is fully patched with no agent, no service and no listening port on the host. It can also work at the firmware or boot menu stage, before any operating system or endpoint protection is running, which is why software-only controls cannot see it. The behaviour is legitimate in some environments, for example a lab or a kiosk that must be managed without an agent, and the risk arises when the device is added without authorisation, often by someone already inside the building, or when a remote worker is sent hardware to plug in at home. Detection is mostly physical, network and procurement work: unauthorised devices appear on the network as a new host with outbound connections to a remote session service, but they may leave no trace inside the monitored operating system beyond a new universal serial bus device appearing in the hardware inventory. Inventory, network admission control and physical inspection are the practical controls, supported by asset records that tie a device to an owner and a purpose.

beginner.definition: This is a small physical box that sits between a computer and its screen, keyboard and mouse. It sends the picture over the network and passes your typing back to the computer. In effect, someone far away can use the machine as if they were sitting at it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Software on the computer cannot see this box, because the box pretends to be an ordinary keyboard and screen. It can even control the machine while it starts up, before the operating system loads. An attacker who plugs one in does not need to install anything and does not need a stolen password. It is useful for administrators in special cases, which is why a company may need a rule about who may bring one in.
howItWorks: The attacker connects the small appliance to the computer's video output and its keyboard and mouse ports.
The computer detects ordinary hardware, so it installs no agent and shows no unusual running program.
The appliance joins the network, by cable or wireless, and usually asks for an address automatically.
It connects out to a remote service or is reached on a port, and streams the screen to the operator.
The operator sends keystrokes and mouse movements back, and the computer treats them as local input.
The session works even during startup, so security software that has not loaded yet cannot block it.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk where visitors must sign in, but contractors working on the building come through a side corridor with their own key. That key was issued to a real contractor for a real job, and the corridor is not covered by the main camera. A person with such a key never passes the desk, so the visitor book stays clean. The entry is real and authorised in form, but nothing ties it to the person using it tonight.
takeaways: Hardware remote access can control a computer with no software installed on it.
Software-only monitoring will not detect this, so asset and network checks matter.
Control who may attach peripherals physically, and keep records tying each device to an owner.

objectives: Explain how an IP-based keyboard, video and mouse appliance controls a computer remotely.
Describe why host-based security software may not detect this kind of remote access.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from software-based remote access in the parent technique.
Identify the network and hardware inventory evidence an unauthorised device leaves behind.
Outline policy controls that limit unauthorised physical remote access devices.
